title: Most invoicing US small businesses carry invoices overdue 30+ days, and manual payment processes compound the cash-flow scramble

history.reason: Initial evidence collected in the first discovery session (issue #7)
Added independent Federal Reserve survey evidence from PR #10 (claude-code-cloud); answers the open question on independent corroboration only in part. Status unchanged.
Integration correction: removed stale no-independent-source language after PR10 Fed addition; retained distinct denominators and unresolved willingness to pay.

description: US small businesses that sell on invoice terms routinely wait past 30 days to be paid: 59% carried invoices overdue by 30+ days in Intuit QuickBooks' 2026 survey, owed $17,700 on average. The administrative core of the problem is the manual chase-and-wait cycle — following up on invoices, matching bills, approvals, reminders, and record-keeping — which businesses themselves name as the top internal cause of their own delayed payments, on top of payment-processing delays after customers do pay. Even small missed payments (under $1,000 for 12% of owners) can make payroll or bills hard to cover.
customer_segment: US small businesses (surveyed population: owners of businesses with 0-250 employees) that issue invoices or sell on terms — services, trades, and other B2B sellers. The source is cross-industry; which segments carry the worst load is unknown.
context: Payment terms are a structural driver: businesses on net-30 terms report overdue invoices at roughly double the rate of businesses requiring immediate payment. Late money in becomes late money out — 42% of businesses say outside pressures delayed payments they owed to their own contractors, suppliers, or vendors.

evidence.text: 59% of surveyed businesses have invoices overdue by 30+ days (up from 47% the prior year); businesses with unpaid invoices are owed $17,700 on average.
39% of owners say a single late payment made it hard to cover payroll or bills in the past year; 12% said a late payment under $1,000 was enough to cause strain.
Manual processes are the number-one internal reason businesses give for delayed outgoing payments, and 74% are not fully automated in managing and paying bills.
49% of owners say standard payment processing times create critical or moderate cash-flow gaps even after the customer has paid.

Federal Reserve Banks' 2024 Report on Payments (2023 Small Business Credit Survey; N=4,858 employer firms with 1-499 employees): 39% of firms said customers are slow to pay, 20% cited time-consuming processes such as billing customers and making deposits, and 18% cited delays in settlement or availability of funds; slow-paying customers are more common among firms that collect payment after delivery, on a schedule, in installments or through a third party.

alternatives: Requiring immediate or upfront payment and deposits (strongly associated with having no overdue invoices)
Manual follow-up calls and emails (status quo chase)
Paying instant-transfer/fast-deposit fees to access earned money (59% paid extra fees last year)
Credit cards and lines of credit as gap-fillers

contradictory_evidence.text: Much of the problem is mitigated by a terms choice: 64% of businesses with no overdue invoices require immediate payment, versus 34% of businesses with overdue invoices — so a segment of sellers has already opted out of the worst of it, where their market allows.

The invoice-overdue percentages and balances come from Intuit vendor research. Federal Reserve evidence now provides independent directional corroboration of payment challenges, but does not replicate those vendor-specific measures or dollar amounts.

Independent corroboration is partial: the Fed survey reproduces the direction (slow-paying customers is the second most common payments challenge) but measures reported challenges, not invoices overdue 30+ days, so it does not reproduce the vendor study's 59% or its dollar amounts. Fees (52%) were a more common challenge than slow payment (39%), 20% of firms reported no payments challenge, the payments module is opt-in, and no cost or willingness-to-pay data exist.

uncertainty: Vendor self-report measures overdue-invoice incidence and balances; the independent Federal Reserve survey measures payment challenges in a different employer-firm population. Neither quantifies owner hours spent chasing payments here, proves causality from manual work to overdue invoices, or establishes willingness to buy a new solution.
open_questions: How many hours per week do owners or staff actually spend chasing and reconciling payments?
Which segments (trades, agencies, professional services) carry the highest overdue shares and balances?
Where exactly does the manual work sit: reminders, bill matching, approvals, or reconciliation?
Do independent sources (Federal Reserve SBCS, NFIB) reproduce the 59% / $17.7K picture?
next_actions: Use the existing Federal Reserve payments evidence as partial corroboration; seek independent segment-specific time/cost and purchasing evidence before deepening.
Find segment-specific sources for trades/field services.
